multipleTestingNote: 10 pre-registered event(s) x 7 horizons = 70 cells screened. P-values are NOT corrected for multiple testing; treat a single green cell among many as weak evidence.

events.name: GLD oversold washout below its 200-day SMA
events.rationale: A mean-reversion proxy, NOT a replication of the SentimenTrader GLD study (which rests on a proprietary Optix sentiment index and a 21-year seasonal window we cannot reproduce). Mechanism: a liquid, widely-held commodity ETF that becomes acutely oversold (RSI below 30) while already trading below its 200-day SMA has usually overshot on momentum or forced selling, so a partial snap-back toward the mean is common over the following weeks. Deliberately a COUNTER-TREND test, logged as such, not a trend signal. Forward returns on GLD; significance from our random-entry Monte Carlo; thin-sample caveat applies.
events.summary: Buy GLD when RSI(14) drops below 30 while it is already under its 200-day average. On our data the washout does NOT reliably bounce: 12 episodes, no horizon significant, and the 3-month edge is negative. Counter-trend by design and thin-sampled — context, not a signal.
events.definition: Trigger on the session GLD's RSI(14) crosses below 30 while GLD closes below its 200-day SMA. Forward returns measured on GLD from the trigger close.
events.entryNote: Forward return measured from the close of the trigger day (event-study convention).

events.name: SLV oversold washout below its 200-day SMA
events.rationale: The same oversold-in-downtrend mean-reversion construct as the GLD card, applied to silver to test whether the washout-bounce holds across precious metals. Silver (SLV) is higher-beta and more volatile than gold, so washouts run deeper and snap-backs are larger but noisier; the natural robustness check on the gold result. Counter-trend by design. Forward returns on SLV; significance from our random-entry Monte Carlo; thin-sample caveat applies.
events.summary: The same oversold-in-downtrend rule on silver, as the robustness check on the gold card. Higher beta means deeper washouts and larger but noisier snap-backs: 16 episodes, best cell +11.8pp at 6 months (p=0.08) — suggestive, not established, and the sample is thin.
events.definition: Trigger on the session SLV's RSI(14) crosses below 30 while SLV closes below its 200-day SMA. Forward returns measured on SLV from the trigger close.
events.entryNote: Forward return measured from the close of the trigger day (event-study convention).

events.name: S&P 500 strong 2nd quarter → 9-month forward
events.rationale: A strong second quarter — a price gain in each of April, May and June, and/or a quarterly price gain of 10 per cent or more from the end of March to the end of June — is a momentum-and-participation regime signal. Broad, sustained strength into mid-year has historically been followed by above-base-rate S&P 500 price returns over the following nine months (June close to the following March close). This is not a replication of the SentimenTrader record, which is a proprietary lead re-tested here on our own data; the card reports OUR numbers only. The honest edge is the excess over the unconditional nine-month base rate — the S&P 500 is already positive over roughly four in five nine-month windows — not the raw win rate, and signals cluster in secular bull markets, so the effective sample is thinner than the raw count. A long-only seasonal context signal, judged on our random-entry Monte Carlo, with a thin-sample caveat carried on the card.
events.summary: A strong second quarter (up in April, May and June, and/or +10% across the quarter) as a momentum-and-participation regime signal. 22 instances; the honest edge is the excess over the base rate, not the raw win rate — +5.3pp at 6 months (p=0.04). Signals cluster in secular bulls, so the effective sample is thinner than 22 suggests.
events.definition: At each June month-end, flag a 'strong' 2nd quarter when the S&P 500 posts a price gain in each of April, May and June, and/or gains 10% or more from the end of March to the end of June. Forward returns measured on the S&P 500 price index from the June close over 3/6/9/12 months (9M is the headline: June close to the following March close).
events.entryNote: Forward return measured on the monthly price index from the June month-end close (event-study convention).
events.carriedReason: GSPC is sourced locally (Norgate) and is not available to this run

events.name: S&P 500 from end-July of a midterm election year
events.gateOverrideNote: Capped to MONITOR: the full-sample 6M significance (p=0.01) is a PRE-1974 artefact — modern (1974-2022, n=13) 6M is only +2.7%, ~base-rate, and the edge does not transfer to the Nasdaq. Seasonal context, not a live edge.
events.rationale: A calendar-cycle seasonal: in a US MIDTERM election year (year mod 4 = 2), enter the S&P 500 at the end-of-July close and measure forward price-index returns. Prompted by a SentimenTrader lead re-tested on OUR data (Norgate $SPX monthly, 1949+); OUR numbers only, never the vendor's prose or figures. Mechanism: the four-year presidential cycle — post-midterm gridlock giving way to pre-election-year stimulus — historically made the stretch from the midterm-year autumn into the following year the strongest of the cycle. FULL-SAMPLE RESULT (19 midterm years, 1950-2022): August and the autumn are unremarkable (1M +1.5%, 3M +2.6%, no edge — the midterm dip); the 6-month window through end-January is +12.7% median, +7.6pp over base and significant (p=0.01); 12M was positive in all 19 at +17.3% median (the 100% flattered by the S&P's high unconditional 12M positive rate, p=0.07). DOWNGRADED OUT OF ACT (analyst-capped to MONITOR) — the full-sample edge does NOT hold up under two robustness checks. (1) SPLIT BY ERA: restricting to modern midterm years (1974-2022, n=13) collapses the headline 6M from +12.7% to just +2.7% — essentially the base rate; the entire significant edge is carried by six pre-1974 instances (1950-1970). (2) CROSS-INDEX: the identical trigger on the Nasdaq (Composite 1971+, n=13; Nasdaq-100 1985+, n=10) shows NO 6M edge (Composite 6M edge -2.3pp, p=0.49; its autumn is if anything significantly weaker, 3M -6.4pp, p=0.05), and on the common 1974-2022 period the S&P and the Nasdaq are near-identical and both weak. A genuine cycle effect would transfer across correlated indices and survive out of its original era; this does neither, so the 6M significance is a pre-1974, S&P-sample artefact rather than a robust edge. Retained as SEASONAL CONTEXT, not a signal — the honest modern expectation is roughly base-rate with a weak-to-negative autumn. 2026 is a midterm year, so the instance is live, but read it as context only.
events.summary: Enter the S&P 500 at end-July of a US midterm election year. The full-sample 6-month edge looks strong (+7.6pp, p=0.01) but does NOT survive an era split: restricted to 1974 onward the headline collapses from +12.7% to +2.7%, roughly the base rate, and the same rule shows no edge on the Nasdaq. Analyst-capped out of ACT — a pre-1974 artefact, kept as context.
events.definition: At each end-of-July month-end in a year where year mod 4 = 2 (a US midterm election year: ..., 2014, 2018, 2022, 2026), measure forward S&P 500 price-index returns over 1/3/6/12 months. The 6-month window (end-July to end-January) is the headline. Forward returns on the Norgate $SPX monthly series from the July close (event-study convention).
events.entryNote: Forward return measured on the monthly price index from the end-of-July close of a midterm election year (event-study convention).
events.carriedReason: GSPC is sourced locally (Norgate) and is not available to this run

events.name: Bitcoin — 1-week volatility thrust (+2σ)
events.rationale: A volatility-normalised thrust: a ~1-week (5 trading day) move measured in units of the instrument's OWN prior volatility, so a large move in a calm regime scores higher than the same move in a violent one. Trigger at +2 sigma or more. CAUSAL by construction — the 60-day vol denominator is measured over the window ENDING BEFORE the return window opens, so no part of the move being scored sits inside its own benchmark. Mechanism: a move large relative to recent vol signals a genuine repricing or participation shift rather than noise, and such thrusts have shown SHORT-horizon continuation. Prompted by a charted observation of Bitcoin weekly sigma moves and rebuilt entirely on OUR data with OUR threshold; the card reports OUR numbers only. THE TESTED EDGE IS SHORT — about 4 weeks (the thesis horizon here); a separate private walk-forward found the 1-month edge is where the signal lives, while the most EXTREME thrusts (+4 sigma and above) showed NO medium-term edge and a negative 3-6 month tilt, i.e. bigger is NOT better. Read the 1M column first. MULTIPLE-TESTING WARNING: this same signal is deliberately run across several instruments as a cross-asset robustness check, so treat any single green cell among them as weak evidence — the question is whether the effect appears CONSISTENTLY, not whether one asset prints a low p. CROSS-ASSET TEST (the decisive check, run on OUR data before publishing): the SAME signal was run on six instruments. It holds across crypto — Bitcoin +6.8pp 1M edge (p=0.00), Ethereum +5.8pp (p=0.10), Solana +10.4pp (p=0.07) — but VANISHES in large-cap equities: NVIDIA +0.7pp (p=0.73), Apple -0.4pp (p=0.74), Nasdaq-100 -0.0pp (p=0.96), and those equity samples are the LARGEST of the set (n=82-102), so the null is well-powered, not underpowered. TWO CONSEQUENCES, both carried honestly: (1) this is a CRYPTO-specific effect (plausibly retail momentum-chasing, thinner liquidity, no circuit breakers), NOT a general volatility-thrust principle — it failed the generalisation test; (2) the crypto agreement is WEAKER than three-for-three implies, because Bitcoin, Ethereum and Solana are highly correlated and in the current live instance all three triggered on the SAME DAY — the effective independent sample is closer to one asset than three. Ethereum and Solana cards were deliberately NOT published for exactly that reason (they would triple-count one bet); the Nasdaq-100 card is published alongside this one as the CONTROL. RECONCILING THE TWO SETS OF NUMBERS: the cross-asset figures above were computed on each instrument's FULL available history (Nasdaq-100 n=82 back to 2000, Apple/NVIDIA n=87-102), which is why they differ from the episode count shown ON this card. The published cards deliberately run on the automated pipeline's 10-year daily window instead, so they stay AUTO-REFRESHED daily rather than depending on a hand-run fetch — a live daily signal must never sit on stale data. On that shorter window the finding is unchanged in direction: Bitcoin 1M edge +6.4pp (p=0.01), Nasdaq-100 -1.3pp (p=0.19). The longer-history equity test is the better-powered evidence for the null; the card is the sustainably-refreshed version of the same result. THIS INSTRUMENT: the ORIGINAL observation and the reference case; crypto's high unconditional drift means the edge over its own baseline is the only meaningful read.
events.summary: A ~1-week move measured in units of Bitcoin's own prior volatility, triggered at +2 sigma, causal by construction. The one signal here with a real short-horizon edge: 51 episodes, +6.4pp over its own base rate at 1 month (p=0.01). But a cross-asset test showed it is CRYPTO-ONLY — it vanishes in large-cap equities on the largest samples of the set. Read the Nasdaq-100 control card beside this one.
events.definition: Trigger when the 5-trading-day return divided by the instrument's prior 60-day daily-return standard deviation (scaled to the 5-day window) reaches +2.0 or more, de-clustered to one episode per 10 sessions. Forward returns measured on the instrument from the trigger close.
events.entryNote: Forward return measured from the close of the trigger day (event-study convention).

events.name: AAII Bull Ratio 20-week MA crosses 48 → Nasdaq 100
events.rationale: A contrarian sentiment signal: the AAII Bull Ratio — bulls / (bulls + bears) from the weekly American Association of Individual Investors survey, a PUBLIC series we hold from 1987 — smoothed by a 20-week average and crossing up through 48 for the first time in six months. Mechanism: retail sentiment recovering from pessimism, which historically occurs after a bear market has played out. Prompted by a SentimenTrader lead and rebuilt entirely on OUR data; the card reports OUR numbers only, never the vendor's prose or figures. CAUSALITY: each reading is consumed on its EFFECTIVE date (when it was actually obtainable, per the register-45 rule in sentiment-composite), never its survey Thursday, and entry is the first close STRICTLY AFTER that — the release lags its stamp by 1-4 days, so using the survey date would buy on information nobody had. OUR RESULT — AND WHY THIS IS PUBLISHED AS CONTEXT, NOT A SIGNAL. We REPRODUCE the vendor's headline almost exactly: 12-month median +22.7% against their stated 22.8%, and 18 of 18 positive. So the implementation is not in dispute. What the lead omits is the denominator: the Nasdaq 100's UNCONDITIONAL 12-month median is +17.9% with an 83% win rate, so the 'exceptional' figure is an edge of just +4.9pp at p=0.42 — nowhere near significant. Shorter horizons are weaker still (1M +1.5pp p=0.32, 3M +1.6pp p=0.52, 6M +0.3pp p=0.91). THE DECISIVE CHECK is like-for-like on another index: run the identical rule on the S&P 500 and the 12-month edge is +0.5pp at p=0.90 — nothing. A signal carrying genuine information about equity sentiment would not vanish when the index changes; the Nasdaq number is that index's drift, and selecting the highest-drift major index is what produces the headline. The 100% win rate is the most persuasive-looking and least informative statistic here: against an 83% base, 18 of 18 is roughly a 3.5% coincidence IF the observations were independent, which they are not — they are regime-clustered with overlapping forward windows. With 20 signals spanning 1989-2025 this is a WELL-POWERED NULL, not an underpowered miss, which makes the finding stronger rather than weaker. Retained as sentiment CONTEXT and as a live base-rate worked example. The lead's second leg (a proprietary corporate-insider indicator, also cited at a 100% 12-month win rate) is unbuildable here and is deliberately excluded rather than assumed.
events.summary: A contrarian retail-sentiment signal: the AAII Bull Ratio's 20-week average crossing above 48. We reproduce the vendor's headline almost exactly (12-month median +22.7% versus their 22.8%, 18 of 18 positive) — and it still says nothing, because the Nasdaq's UNCONDITIONAL 12-month median is +17.9%. That leaves an edge of +4.8pp at p=0.42, and the identical rule on the S&P 500 gives +0.5pp at p=0.90. Published as a live base-rate worked example, not a signal.
events.definition: Trigger when the 20-week moving average of the AAII Bull Ratio (bulls / (bulls + bears)) crosses up through 48, de-clustered to the first such cross in 26 weeks. Entry at the first Nasdaq 100 close strictly after the reading's effective (obtainable) date. Forward returns measured on the Nasdaq 100 price index from that close.
events.entryNote: Forward return measured from the close of the trigger day (event-study convention).

events.name: First policy-rate hike of a cycle → S&P 500
events.rationale: VERDICT FIRST. Since 1994 the S&P 500 has been LOWER a month after the first policy-rate step of a cycle in six instances out of six, against an unconditional base rate of being higher 64% of the time. The median is -3.30% where the base is +1.33%, an edge of -4.63pp at p=0.023. It is published as MONITOR rather than ACT, and the reasons are set out below rather than buried: six episodes in 32 years, an uncorrected p-value, and a real part of the move sitting in the single session after the announcement. THE MECHANICAL DETECTOR IS THE POINT. This card was prompted by a research note whose event list was hand-picked, with no stated rule admitting a date — and a curated list cannot be audited. So the list is replaced rather than consumed. The US bank prime loan rate steps in discrete increments that track the fed funds TARGET, is publicly observable at the time, and needs no judgement about what counts as a cycle start. The effective fed funds rate was tried first and is unusable: it is a market rate that wanders daily, giving 1,520 step-ups above 10bp since 1980 and recovering only three cycle starts, against prime's six of six. THAT SUBSTITUTION CHANGED THE ANSWER, WHICH IS WHY IT MATTERS. Inside the same 1994-2026 window the mechanical rule finds SIX cycle starts where the note listed five. The one it omits is March 1997, the first hike after a two-year pause. On the note's other legs that single event is decisive: on our data the claim that gold rallies after a first hike carries a six-month edge of +6.3pp on the five hand-picked dates and +1.5pp (p=0.81) once 1997 is included, and the three-month edge falls from +2.4pp to +0.4pp (p=0.94). A result that moves by nearly five percentage points on one observation is a property of which dates were chosen. Neither of that note's other two legs is published here; only the equity leg survived, and it survived on the mechanical list, not the curated one. CAUSALITY. Prime is stamped by its effective date, which already lags the FOMC announcement by one session — verified on the March 2022 case, where the decision was announced on the 16th and prime prints its new level on the 17th. Entry at the step-date close is therefore causal: the decision had been public since the previous afternoon, and no part of the entry bar informs the trigger. WHERE THE EFFECT ACTUALLY LIVES. At one month, and not across the one-to-three-month span the prompting note framed. The edge is -4.63pp at one month (p=0.023, 0 of 6 higher) and -6.26pp at two months (p=0.023), then decays: -6.88pp at three months (p=0.042, 2 of 6 higher), -2.12pp at six months (p=0.635) and nothing at a year. Drawdown is the consistent part — a median worst-drawdown of -5.2% inside the first month against a median best-gain of +0.5%. SPECIFICATION SENSITIVITY, REPORTED RATHER THAN SMOOTHED. Two robustness checks bear on how much weight this carries. Delaying entry by one session cuts the one-month edge from -4.63pp to -3.26pp and takes p from 0.023 to 0.09, so roughly a fifth of the measured effect sits in the first session after the announcement and would be hard to capture. Extending the window back to 1980, which adds two more cycle starts, gives -4.09pp at p=0.02 with 1 of 8 higher — the one-month direction survives, and the three-month cell does not (-4.07pp, p=0.12). The one-month direction is the robust part across every specification tested; the magnitude and the longer horizons are not. WHY MONITOR AND NOT ACT. The mechanical gate scores this 7 of 10, which would read ACT. It is capped by an explicit analyst override, logged on the card, for three reasons the gate cannot see. Six episodes in 32 years, recurring roughly every five years, so this card is dormant almost all of the time and its sample cannot pin the magnitude within a factor of two. The p-value is uncorrected and is one of roughly 24 cells screened while the study was built, so it does not clear our own multiple-testing discipline. And the finding is consensus macro rather than a discovery — that equities wobble after the first hike is widely believed, and reproducing a widely-held belief is not the same as having an edge. THE FIRST CARD ON THIS BOOK SCORED ON A FALL. Every other study here predicts the target rising, and until this card was built the credibility gate silently assumed that was universal: it scanned only horizons with a POSITIVE edge for its best p-value and scored consistency as the share of horizons with a positive edge. A study whose finding is a decline therefore scored zero on both and would have rendered IGNORE beside its own strongest cell — this card would have shown 3 of 10. The direction is now declared in the catalogue BEFORE the numbers are computed, never inferred from them, because reading the sign off the results would let the gate keep whichever direction happened to score better and would quietly double the multiple-testing surface of every card on the book. READ IT AS RISK, NOT AS A TRADE. The honest use is as context on a known macro event — the month after a cycle's first hike has been a poor risk-reward window in a small sample, consistently in direction and unreliably in size. It is not a timing rule, and the card carries no trading mandate.
events.summary: A macro-policy event rather than a price signal, and the first card on the book scored on a FALL. When the US bank prime rate makes its first step up after a year-long pause — a mechanical stand-in for the first Fed hike of a cycle — the S&P 500 was lower a month later in six of six instances since 1994, against a 64% base rate of being higher. Edge -4.6pp at p=0.03. Published as MONITOR, not ACT: six episodes in 32 years, an uncorrected p-value, and about a fifth of the effect sits in the single session after the announcement.
events.definition: Trigger when the US bank prime loan rate makes its first step up of more than 10 basis points after at least 252 trading days with no such step — a mechanical stand-in for the first Federal Reserve hike of a tightening cycle. Entry at the S&P 500 close on the step date. Forward returns measured on the S&P 500 price index from that close. Window from 1994, which is also the window the unconditional base rate is drawn from, so events and base are like-for-like.
events.gateOverrideNote: Capped by the analyst. The gate cannot see three things that bear on this card: six episodes in 32 years recurring roughly every five years, so it is dormant almost always; the p-value is uncorrected and one of about 24 cells screened while building it; and the 3-month cell is specification-sensitive, clearing 0.05 only on the primary entry convention. The one-month direction is the robust part, and MONITOR is the honest ceiling for it.
events.entryNote: Forward return measured from the close of the trigger day (event-study convention).
events.carriedReason: GSPC, USPRIME is sourced locally (Norgate) and is not available to this run

events.name: NYSE new lows + weak 200-day breadth, index near its high → S&P 500
events.rationale: VERDICT FIRST, AND IT IS NOT THE ONE THE SOURCE CLAIMS. This signal does not predict lower returns in the near term. It predicts WORSE ODDS. Three months after a trigger the S&P 500 has been higher only 50% of the time against a 70% base rate — a 20pp deterioration at p=0.05 — while the median three-month return is statistically indistinguishable from base. At one month the median is actually 1.8pp ABOVE base (p=0.04), so the index has typically kept rising for a while first. Read it as a change in the distribution of outcomes, not as a top call. WHY THIS LEAD IS DIFFERENT. Every threshold is published: new highs below 21%, breadth at or under 49.75%, index within 4.5% of its high, re-armed when new lows fall under 10%. Nothing proprietary, no hand-picked list of dates, no judgement about what counts as an instance. That is rare enough to say plainly — this card implements someone else's stated rule rather than reconstructing one, and the rule can therefore be audited rather than guessed at. THE THRESHOLDS ARE NOT CURVE-FIT, WHICH WAS CHECKED BEFORE BUILDING. A level like 49.75% looks fitted, so it was tested as such: their exact levels, round numbers (20 and 50), and our own percentiles of the same two series (25 and 49). All three produce 24 raw signals on near-identical dates with near-identical results. A fitted boundary does not survive being moved, and this one does. THE FINDING LIVES IN THE SHAPE, AND THE MEDIAN CANNOT SEE IT. Positive-outcome rates against base: 1M 67% vs 64%, 2M 56% vs 68%, 3M 50% vs 70%, 6M 67% vs 74%, 1Y 67% vs 81%. The three-month cell is a 20pp drop at p=0.05 and the one-year cell a 14pp drop at p=0.07, while every median edge over the same horizons sits between -1.1pp and -4.1pp and none is significant. The source's own asymmetry claim also reproduces on our data: the probability of a 5% drawdown within three months rises from 33% to 48%, while the probability of a 5% gain falls from 53% to 48%. SO THE GATE SCORES THIS CARD ON HIT RATE, AND THAT IS DECLARED. The credibility gate scored significance and consistency off the median until this card, which made it structurally blind to exactly this kind of study — the trap our own discipline notes name, arriving for real. The catalogue now carries a `scoreOn` field, read before the numbers exist for the same reason `direction` is: letting the gate keep whichever statistic scored better would be metric-fishing, and would double the multiple-testing surface of every card on the book. DISCLOSURE: for THIS card the declaration is retrospective, because the numbers were seen first. Every future card declares it in advance, and the regression test refuses a card that leaves it unset and then benefits. WHAT THE DE-CLUSTERING CHECK KILLED, REPORTED BECAUSE IT NEARLY BECAME THE HEADLINE. On raw signals the two-week edge is +1.55pp at p=0.01 and the one-year edge -9.29pp at p=0.01. Both are artefacts of clustering — six signals fell inside fourteen months in 2014-15 and three inside three months in late 2021 — and both vanish once episodes are de-clustered. The hit-rate deterioration is what survives, and it survives at every de-clustering window tested. LIMITS, AND THEY ARE REAL. The sample is 19 independent episodes from 1990, which is the best of any lead tested this year but still small for a quarterly horizon. Norgate's breadth series begin in 1990, whereas the source charts instances back to 1973-74, so this is a PARTIAL reproduction and the earliest cases cannot be checked here. Our series are NYSE COMPOSITE, which includes closed-end funds, bond funds, ADRs and preferreds; the source specifies common stocks for the 200-day condition, so if its universe is common-only the two series differ in level and some signal dates may differ with them. Regime scores zero because the regime tag is built from a series starting in 2016, leaving twelve of nineteen episodes untagged — a known limitation shared with other cards, not a property of this one. HOW TO USE IT. As a risk gauge, not a signal. The honest statement is that a quarter beginning at one of these triggers has historically been a materially worse bet than an average quarter — fewer positive outcomes and a markedly higher chance of a 5% drawdown along the way — without the expected return being reliably lower. That is a reason to size smaller or tighten risk, not a reason to be short, and the card carries no trading mandate. SISTER CARD. `spx-newlow-spike` measures the same phenomenon on S&P 500 members with a different construction. Of its de-clustered signals since 1990, 43% fall within a month of one of this card's signals and the rest fire on different dates. Its three-month median effect is stable across de-clustering windows where this card's is not, so it is the stronger of the two on that statistic. When both fire together, treat them as two measurements of one phenomenon, not as two independent confirmations.
events.summary: A breadth divergence, and the first card whose finding is distributional rather than a median effect. When NYSE new lows expand while fewer than half of stocks hold their 200-day average — yet the S&P 500 still sits within 4.5% of its 252-day high — the index has been higher three months later only 50% of the time against a 70% base rate, a drop of 20pp at p=0.05. It does NOT call a top: the median one-month return is actually ABOVE base. What deteriorates is the odds, and the chance of a 5% drawdown inside three months rises from 33% to 48%.
events.definition: Trigger when all four conditions hold: the percentage of NYSE new highs (as a share of new highs plus new lows) crosses below 21%; the percentage of NYSE stocks above their 200-day moving average is at or below 49.75%; the S&P 500 is within 4.5% of its 252-day high; and the signal has been re-armed by the percentage of new lows falling below 10% since the previous trigger. Entry at the S&P 500 close on the trigger day. Episodes de-clustered at 63 sessions.

events.rationale: VERDICT. At three months this is the strongest breadth result the book carries, and it is stronger than its source claims. The S&P 500 has been higher three months after a trigger in 35% of cases, against a 66% base rate (−31pp, p=0.01). The median three-month return sits 5.5pp below base (−2.9% against +2.6%, p=0.01). Both hold at every de-clustering window tested (63, 126 and 252 sessions), and the hit-rate edge is negative at all seven horizons. WHERE THE SOURCE IS WRONG. The note says the damage shows within one month, with drawdowns beyond 5% outpacing gains beyond 5%. At one month there is nothing to measure: hit rate −2.5pp (p=0.62), median −0.3pp (p=0.77). The effect is real and sits two months later than claimed. That is the same pattern as the NYSE breadth card, which is also right that something is there and wrong about when. THE RULE WAS PUBLISHED IN FULL. Every threshold is stated in the source, nothing is proprietary, and no curated list of dates is involved. Our implementation reproduces the source's own trigger dates, including 2026-05-11 and the latest on 2026-09-24. The companion model in the same note, a proprietary composite risk warning, cannot be built here and is not tested. HOW IT RELATES TO THE NYSE BREADTH CARD. The idea is the same one behind `nyse-riskoff-divergence`: breadth deteriorating underneath an index that still sits near its high. It is not the same signal, though. Of this rule's de-clustered signals since 1990, 43% fall within a month of an NYSE-card signal and the rest fire on different dates. The evidence also differs. The NYSE card's three-month median effect flips sign across de-clustering windows, so that card is scored on hit rate alone, whereas this card's median effect is stable. Read the two as two measurements of one phenomenon. When both fire together they are not two independent confirmations. SCORING, DECLARED IN ADVANCE. The gate scores this card on hit rate, and it is declared in the catalogue as for every card. This time the declaration was made before any number was computed: the pre-registration named hit rate as the primary statistic and the median as secondary. The NYSE card's declaration had to be disclosed as retrospective; this one does not. The mechanical gate reaches ACT 8 of 10 with no override. It is the first card on the book to reach ACT on a predicted fall. The three-month hit-rate p-value of 0.006 still clears 0.05 after a Bonferroni correction across all seven horizons. LIMITS. Eighteen episodes, from 1966. The series runs back to 1960, but the rule fired only three times before 1990, so thirty years of extra history add little evidence. Those three were negative at one and three months, but three observations prove nothing. Regime scores zero because the regime tag comes from a series that starts in 2016 and leaves twelve of eighteen episodes untagged. That is a known limitation shared with other cards. It pulls this card's score down, not up. Only the three-month horizon is individually significant; the others are negative on hit rate without clearing p<0.10 on their own. HOW TO USE IT. Treat it as a risk gauge. It carries no trading mandate. On the record, a quarter that begins at one of these triggers has been a markedly worse bet than an average quarter: roughly one chance in three of ending higher instead of two in three, with a median shortfall of about five points. The index has usually held up for the first month. The case this supports is for sizing down or tightening risk over the following quarter, not for a short position.
events.summary: The strongest breadth result on the book. When the share of S&P 500 members at a new 52-week low spikes above 7.7% while the index is still within 5% of its high, the S&P has been higher three months later only 35% of the time against a 66% base rate: a 31-point drop at p=0.01. The median three-month return is also 5.5 points below base (p=0.01), and both results hold however the episodes are de-clustered. The source's claim that the damage shows within one month does not reproduce, because the effect sits at three months.
events.definition: Trigger when the percentage of S&P 500 members at a new 52-week low crosses above 7.7% while the S&P 500 is within 5% of its 252-day high. After a trigger the rule re-arms only once that percentage has fallen below 0.5%. The percentage uses the day's actual member count (advances + declines + unchanged) as its denominator, not a fixed 500. Entry is the S&P 500 close on the trigger day. Episodes are de-clustered at 63 sessions.
